title: The minimum viable product
blurb: Explain what an MVP is for, how it differs from a first release with everything, and where it appears in PRINCE2 Agile.
question: A sponsor wants the first release of a new ordering portal to contain every requested feature 'so customers are impressed'. The chief product owner proposes an MVP instead. What is an MVP for, and why is it the better first step?

teach.h: The smallest thing that teaches you the most
teach.body: The purpose of a minimum viable product (MVP) is to create a basic version of a product with minimal cost and time, so the team can gather early feedback. It usually holds the essential features, which are then refined according to user feedback throughout the project. An MVP is not a complete product: it is an initial version that lets the team learn and iterate before full-scale development.

teach.h: MVP versus a first release with everything

teach.caption: Lean Startup calls a loop like this build-measure-learn (background, not PRINCE2 Agile wording).

teach.h: Why PRINCE2 Agile values the MVP
teach.body: In PRINCE2 Agile the MVP helps assess product viability by testing core features with minimal investment. How it is defined varies with the level of uncertainty: in highly innovative contexts it often means exploring key assumptions and validating them as quickly as possible. It supports the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, alongside a value focus, the project canvas and frequent releases that bring benefits earlier.

items.label: MVP: reorder from past orders, pay on account

teach.caption: Later releases are shaped by what users did with the MVP.

teach.body: Copperleaf Foods, a bakery-ingredient maker, is building a trade ordering portal. The sponsor wants all 40 requested features in the first release. Chief product owner Hannah Fischer proposes an MVP instead: reorder from past orders and pay on account, released to 20 pilot bakeries. Feedback shows customers value choosing a delivery slot far more than the recipe library, so the backlog is reprioritized. The MVP is named on the project canvas so a late forecast would trigger an exception.

teach.text: An MVP is not a cut-down finished product or 'version one with everything'. It is the least you can build to learn whether core assumptions hold. 'Minimum viability' in the fix-and-flex table is a related but different idea: the floor of benefits the project must achieve, fixed, with flex above it.

items: MVP: a basic version built with minimal cost and time to gather early feedback (6.3.1).
It holds essential features, refined by user feedback; it is not a complete product.
It helps assess product viability by testing core features with minimal investment.
In innovative work it means validating key assumptions quickly.
Name the MVP on the project canvas so a late forecast can trigger an exception.
Agile contracts may define the MVP and its tolerances.

summary: You can now explain the purpose of an MVP and why it is not a complete first release. You can also say where PRINCE2 Agile expects it to be recorded and how it supports continued business justification.

A.q: What is the purpose of a minimum viable product?
options: To deliver the complete product in one release
To prove the board has approved the business case
To get early feedback from a basic, low-cost version
To replace the project canvas once delivery starts
A.why: An MVP is a basic version built with minimal cost and time to gather early feedback (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: An MVP is deliberately not a complete product.
whyNot.1: Board approval is a directing decision; the MVP is about learning from users.
whyNot.3: The project canvas stays as the business justification and should name the MVP.

A.q: Which statement about an MVP is correct?
options: It is a complete product with every feature included
It holds essential features refined by user feedback
It is frozen once released and is not changed
It must contain every Must have and Should have story
A.why: The MVP typically includes essential features that are refined according to user feedback throughout the project (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: An MVP is not a complete product; it is an initial version.
whyNot.2: The point of an MVP is to change it in response to feedback.
whyNot.3: An MVP holds the essential features only; Should haves are flexible scope.

A.q: In which artifact must the MVP be identified, if one is used, so an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be late?
options: Release map
Team dashboard
Risk register
Project canvas
A.why: The project canvas, the agile form of the business case, must identify the MVP (if used) so an exception can be raised if it is forecast late (6.3.2).

whyNot.0: The release map plans releases and features, but the book places this requirement on the project canvas.
whyNot.1: The team dashboard shows team progress and replaces the checkpoint report.
whyNot.2: The risk register records risks; it is not where the MVP is defined.

B.q: In highly innovative contexts, what does defining an MVP often involve?
options: Exploring key assumptions to validate them quickly
Agreeing the full specification before any build
Locking the scope so the board can fix the budget
Delivering every feature to a pilot group at once
B.why: Book 6.3.1: in highly innovative contexts, defining an MVP often involves exploring key assumptions to validate them as quickly as possible.

whyNot.1: A full specification up front is the opposite of learning fast from a basic version.
whyNot.2: Scope is what flexes in PRINCE2 Agile; time and cost are the fixed aspects.
whyNot.3: Delivering every feature at once is a full release, not an MVP.

B.q:
Which two statements about the MVP are correct?
1. It helps assess product viability by testing core features with minimal investment.
2. It is the final release handed over at project closure.
3. A commercial management approach may include a definition of the MVP and its tolerances.
4. It is another name for the project product description.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
B.why: The MVP tests core features with minimal investment (6.3.1), and agile contracts may include a definition of the MVP and tolerances (Table 7.3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the MVP comes early, not at closure.
whyNot.1: Both 2 and 4 are wrong: the MVP is early, and the project backlog replaces the project product description.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the project product description becomes the project backlog, not the MVP.

B.q: A retailer's team plans to release just the core checkout feature to 200 customers to see whether they use it before building more. Which concept is this?
options: Definition of Done
Minimum viable product
Trading and swapping
Refactoring
B.why: Releasing a basic version to real users to test a core feature and learn before building more is an MVP (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: The Definition of Done sets when an item counts as complete; it is not about releasing to learn.
whyNot.2: Trading swaps requirements of similar effort to absorb change.
whyNot.3: Refactoring improves internal structure without changing behaviour.

C.q: Which PRINCE2 principle does the MVP MOST directly support, and how?
options: Continued business justification: it tests value early
Manage by stages: it removes the need for stage boundaries
Define roles: it names who owns each feature
Tailor to suit: it replaces the project brief
C.why: Table 5.1 links the MVP, value focus, the project canvas and frequent releases to ensuring continued business justification.

whyNot.1: Stage boundaries remain in PRINCE2 Agile; the MVP does not remove them.
whyNot.2: Roles are set by the organization practice; the MVP is about product viability.
whyNot.3: The project brief is still produced; the MVP does not replace it.

C.q: Under PRINCE2 Agile fix and flex (Table 3.1), how are benefits treated?
options: Flexed fully, with no minimum level of benefit set
Fixed at the full figure in the business case
Fixed for minimum viability, flexed above it
Zero tolerance, the same as for time and cost
C.why: Table 3.1 fixes benefits for minimum viability and flexes them above it.

whyNot.0: There is a fixed floor: the minimum viability of benefits.
whyNot.1: Only the minimum is fixed; benefits above it can flex.
whyNot.3: Zero tolerance on all levels of plan applies to time and cost, not benefits.

C.q: A board member says the MVP should include every requested feature so users are not disappointed. Why is this inconsistent with PRINCE2 Agile?
options: An MVP must be agreed by the senior supplier first
An MVP belongs to the closing a project process
An MVP is measured in hours rather than features
An MVP is a basic version built for early feedback
C.why: An MVP is a basic version with essential features, built with minimal cost and time to gather early feedback; it is not a complete product (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: The senior supplier provides supplier resources; agreement by that role is not what defines an MVP.
whyNot.1: The MVP is used early to learn; closing a project confirms acceptance and hands over.
whyNot.2: An MVP is defined by its essential features, not by hours.

reteach.title: Test the recipe before opening the restaurant
reteach.question: Would you open a full restaurant with a 40-dish menu before checking whether anyone wants your signature dish?

blocks.body: A chef with a new idea might run a pop-up with three dishes before investing in a full restaurant. Diners' reactions show what to keep, change or drop. The MVP works the same way: the smallest version that real users can try, built quickly and cheaply, so the next decisions rest on evidence instead of guesses.

blocks.text: 'Minimum' does not mean poor quality: an MVP's essential features must still work. It means the least scope that lets you learn.

explain.body: A basic version of a product, built with minimal cost and time, holding the essential features so the team can gather early feedback.

options: the full approved budget
minimal cost and time
every Must and Should story
a fixed set of 40 features
test.why: The MVP is built with minimal cost and time to develop (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: Spending the full budget defeats the point of a minimal first version.
whyNot.2: Should haves are flexible scope; the MVP holds the essentials.
whyNot.3: The MVP is defined by essential features, not a fixed large set.

explain.body: After release, the MVP's essential features are refined according to user feedback throughout the project. That learning shapes the backlog and later releases.

test.q: What happens to the MVP's features after release?
options: They are frozen until project closure
They are handed to operations unchanged
They move to the risk register for review
They are refined according to user feedback
test.why: The MVP's essential features are refined according to user feedback throughout the project (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: Freezing them would throw away the feedback the MVP exists to collect.
whyNot.1: Handover comes at transition to operations, after learning has shaped the product.
whyNot.2: Features are product scope, not risks to record.

explain.body: The project canvas must identify the MVP, if used, so an exception can be raised if it is forecast late. Agile contracts can include a definition of the MVP and tolerances.

test.q: Why must the MVP be identified in the project canvas?
options: So an exception can be raised if it is forecast late
So the team dashboard can show its story points total
So the project board can sign off each team plan in turn
So the tester can skip the Definition of Done
test.why: Naming the MVP on the project canvas means an exception can be raised if its delivery is forecast to be late (6.3.2).

whyNot.1: Story points are shown on burn charts and team dashboards; that is not why the canvas names the MVP.
whyNot.2: The board does not sign off team plans; teams produce them in managing product delivery.
whyNot.3: The Definition of Done still applies to MVP features.

explain.body: An MVP is not a complete product. A first release with every feature costs more, takes longer and delays the feedback that would show whether the core idea works.

test.q: Which is the BEST example of an MVP for a new parcel-tracking app?
options: A full app with tracking, returns and chat support
A tracking-only version released to a pilot group
A detailed specification approved by the board
A design mock-up kept inside the delivery team
test.why: A basic version with the essential feature, put in front of real users for early feedback, is an MVP.

whyNot.0: A full-featured app is a complete product, not a minimum viable one.
whyNot.2: A specification is not a product users can try.
whyNot.3: A mock-up kept inside the team gathers no feedback from real users.
